opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think they're really quite different things. Large language models learn from a huge corpus of text that people have written. They're learning to mimic people, to predict what a person would say next. That's learning from human-generated data, not from the model's own experience of the world.

Learning from experience is what animals do, what we do. You take an action, you see what happens, and you learn from the consequences. There's a goal, there's a reward, and you find out whether what you did was good or bad. That's the essence of reinforcement learning, and to me it's the essence of intelligence.

A language model doesn't really have a goal in that sense. Predicting the next token isn't a goal about the world; it doesn't change anything in the world. And it doesn't get surprised by the world. If something unexpected happens after it says something, it doesn't learn from that, at least not in its normal operation. It has no ground truth about what the right thing to say is. It's just what people would say.

So I'd say the language models are trying to get by without having a model of the world, really. They have a model of what people would say about the world. That's a different thing. A true world model lets you predict what will happen, and then you can check it against what actually happens and learn. That loop of acting, observing, and updating, continually throughout your life, is what I mean by learning from experience. And I think that's going to be what scales in the long run, not imitating humans.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think there's a fundamental difference. Large language models are trained to mimic what people have written. They're predicting the next token in a corpus of text, and what they learn is essentially what humans would say. That's a form of supervised learning, really. It's imitation.

Learning from experience is something quite different. An agent that learns from experience has a goal. It takes actions in the world, it sees what happens as a result, and it adjusts based on whether those outcomes were good or bad for it. There's a reward signal. There's a ground truth about what's right, which is the actual consequences of its actions. The large language models don't have that. There's no notion of what the right thing to say is, other than what a person would have said. There's no goal, and without a goal there's no way to know whether you're doing well or badly, except by appealing to some external human judgment.

And I'd say the other big piece is continual learning. An animal, a child, learns all the time. Every moment, it's updating its model of the world based on what it just experienced. The language models are trained once, in a big batch, and then they're frozen. They don't learn during their normal operation. So they have knowledge, but they don't have the thing I'd call learning in the real sense, which is ongoing adaptation from interacting with the world.

So I'd put it this way. The language models learn from people. Experiential agents learn from the world. And I think the second one is where intelligence actually comes from. It's what we see in nature. No squirrel learns by reading what other squirrels wrote.

astra-6.text:
The key distinction is where the information comes from and what determines whether learning was successful. A language model is primarily trained on examples of what people have said. It learns to predict the next word or token. That’s a kind of learning, certainly, but the experience it’s learning from is largely a record of human activity.

When I talk about learning through experience, I mean an agent interacting with its environment: taking actions, observing the consequences, and learning how to achieve its goals. Its actions affect what happens next, including what information it gets. So the agent has to discover things for itself, and it needs some signal of whether those discoveries help it do better.

For example, you could learn about riding a bicycle by reading everything people have written about it. But when you actually get on the bicycle, you have a different source of information. You lean, you turn the handlebars, you start to fall, and you adjust. You’re learning the consequences of your own actions.

These aren’t mutually exclusive. A language model could be part of a system that acts and learns from the results. The important question is whether it continues to learn from that interaction, rather than depending primarily on knowledge that people have already collected and expressed in language.

sol-6.1.text:
The key distinction is that learning from experience involves acting and observing the consequences. You do something, the world changes, and you get information about whether that was a good thing to do. Your actions affect the data you get next.

With a large language model, most of the learning is from a fixed collection of things that people have written. That’s a tremendously rich source of information, but the model isn’t choosing actions and finding out what happens. It’s learning to predict what someone would say.

Now, predicting is an important part of intelligence. I wouldn’t dismiss that. But we want agents that can discover how the world works and how to achieve goals through their own interaction with it. They should keep learning while they’re operating, rather than having a learning phase followed by a phase in which they just use what they’ve learned.

And these aren’t mutually exclusive. A language model can be part of an agent that learns from experience. The question is whether its learning ultimately comes from the consequences of its own actions, or remains tied to reproducing human-generated data.
